meta.title: TFP — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the Brazilian Society for the Defense of Tradition, Family and Property and of Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira (1908–present)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the TFP — Sociedade Brasileira de Defesa da Tradição, Família e Propriedade, founded in São Paulo on 26 July 1960 by the lay Catholic leader Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira — its campaigns, its international network, the 1985 CNBB note, the post-1995 succession dispute, and the two branches of today: the Heralds of the Gospel and the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset on a religiously and politically contested subject. Four source families are labeled throughout: movement/sympathetic (IPCO, tfp.org, arautos.org), ecclesiastical (CNBB, Vatican), academic (Zanotto, Caldeira, CPDOC-FGV) and critical/press/ex-member accounts. Campaign numbers are the movement's own and are attributed; 'sect' accusations are presented as attributed accusations with the movement's replies; no accusation is asserted as fact. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A lay Catholic traditionalist civic movement founded in São Paulo in 1960 by Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira, known for street campaigns against communism and agrarian reform, and for a network of autonomous sister TFPs on four continents.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 26 July 1960, São Paulo — consensus date across sources; co-founder lists vary slightly.

facts.label: Doctrinal matrix
facts.value: 'Revolução e Contra-Revolução' (1959): Plinio's reading of five centuries of 'Revolution' (pseudo-Reformation → French Revolution → communism) and the 'Counter-Revolution' against it — his technical terms, always attributed to the text.

facts.label: The 1985 CNBB note
facts.value: In April 1985 a CNBB commission declared 'notorious the lack of communion of the TFP with the Church in Brazil', citing 'esoteric character, religious fanaticism, cult of the leader's personality' — the movement published replies; the note's full text circulates mainly via those replies.

facts.label: The split
facts.value: After Plinio's death (1995), the majority wing under João Scognamiglio Clá Dias founded the Heralds of the Gospel (1999, pontifical approval 2001) and won the courts' award of the TFP name (2003–04); the founders' wing created the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira (2006).

facts.label: Today
facts.value: Two branches claiming Plinio's legacy — the Heralds (under a pontifical commissioner since 2019) and the IPCO — plus an active international TFP network (American TFP, TFP France, Piotr Skarga in Poland, and others).

events.title: Birth of Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira
events.text: Born into a traditional paulista family; Jesuit schooling (Colégio São Luís), law at the future USP.

events.title: The Marian Congregations
events.text: Plinio joins São Paulo's Marian Congregations — the milieu from which his group would grow.

events.title: Youngest constituent deputy
events.text: Co-founder of the Liga Eleitoral Católica, Plinio is elected to the National Constituent Assembly on São Paulo's Chapa Única at 24 — the youngest deputy of the Constituinte (sympathetic sources add 'most voted in the country'; attributed). The 1934 Constitution incorporated points of the Catholic platform.

events.title: Director of O Legionário
events.text: Plinio directs the archdiocesan weekly O Legionário — named director in August 1933 per movement sources, effective from about 1935 per Wikipedia; the divergence is recorded. He leaves the paper in 1947.

events.title: President of São Paulo's Catholic Action
events.text: First president of the Archdiocesan Junta of Catholic Action (to 1944).

events.title: 'Em Defesa da Ação Católica'
events.text: Plinio's polemic against 'progressive'/Maritainian currents in Catholic Action, prefaced by nuncio Aloisi Masella — a storm of controversy that begins his estrangement from the paulista curia.

events.title: Break with the curia
events.text: Under the new archbishop Carlos Carmelo de Vasconcelos Motta, Plinio loses the Catholic Action presidency (1944) and the Legionário direction (1947) — ecclesial ostracism. Sympathetic sources highlight a laudatory 1949 letter signed by Msgr. Montini in Pius XII's name; the document is reproduced only by movement sites, so it is recorded as their claim.

events.title: Catolicismo founded
events.text: The monthly Catolicismo is founded under the patronage of Bishop Antônio de Castro Mayer of Campos — the group's platform for the next decade.

events.title: 'Revolução e Contra-Revolução'
events.text: Published in Catolicismo's 100th issue: the movement's doctrinal matrix, reading modern history as a five-century 'Revolution' and calling for a 'Counter-Revolution' — Plinio's technical vocabulary, attributed to the text.

events.title: TFP founded
events.text: The Sociedade Brasileira de Defesa da Tradição, Família e Propriedade is founded; co-founders include Adolpho Lindenberg, Plinio Vidigal Xavier da Silveira and José Fernando de Camargo — the lists vary slightly between sources.

events.title: 'Reforma Agrária: Questão de Consciência'
events.text: Four authors — Bishop Geraldo de Proença Sigaud, Bishop Antônio de Castro Mayer, Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira and the economist Luiz Mendonça de Freitas — publish the anti-agrarian-reform manifesto; about 30,000 copies over four editions (movement figures, attributed).

events.title: The Coetus Internationalis Patrum
events.text: Sigaud, Castro Mayer and Marcel Lefebvre articulate the conservative minority of Vatican II; movement sources describe Plinio as the group's lay strategist — that role rests on sympathetic sources and is attributed.

events.title: The street campaigns
events.text: Caravans under red standards with a golden lion, public rosaries and signature drives against communism and 'socialist and confiscatory' agrarian reform make the TFP a fixture of Brazilian streets.

events.title: The petition to Paul VI
events.text: The 'Message to Paul VI' against 'communist infiltration' in the Church gathers 1,600,368 signatures in Brazil (2,025,201 with the Southern Cone TFPs) — the movement's own numbers, always attributed.

events.title: Sigaud breaks with the TFP
events.text: Archbishop Sigaud breaks with Plinio and the movement, supporting the Médici government's agrarian program and diverging on liturgical-ecclesial questions.

events.title: The international network
events.text: Sister TFPs form in Argentina, Chile and Uruguay (1967), then Spain (1971), the United States (incorporated 18 May 1973 as the Foundation for a Christian Civilization — PT Wikipedia says 1974; the divergence is recorded), Canada (1975), France (1977), Germany (1982) and beyond.

events.title: The Venezuelan crisis
events.text: A press campaign and parliamentary inquiry target the 'Resistencia-TFP', with a member arrested on suspicion of a plot against John Paul II and accusations of being a 'sect'; the accusations never produced a conviction in the sources consulted, the Venezuelan TFP was effectively extinguished by around 1986, and every characterization here is attributed.

events.title: The CNBB note
events.text: A CNBB commission (Bishops Gilberto Pereira Lopes, Antonio Misiara, Carlos Alberto Navarro) declares 'notorious the lack of communion of the TFP with the Church in Brazil', citing 'esoteric character, religious fanaticism, cult of the leader's personality and abusive use of the name of Mary', and exhorts Catholics not to join. The full text circulates mainly via the TFP's own replies — the CNBB original is a documented gap.

events.title: Castro Mayer at Écône — without the TFP
events.text: Castro Mayer co-consecrates Lefebvre's four bishops and incurs the declared excommunication (Ecclesia Dei). The TFP did not accompany him and remained formally in communion — the key TFP ≠ SSPX distinction; Castro Mayer's Campos succession is documented in the fsspx project.

events.title: The French parliamentary report
events.text: Parliamentary report No. 2468 on sects lists the TFP and its associated Avenir de la Culture among 'mouvements sectaires' — a report whose methodology was itself widely contested; both the listing and the criticism of the report are recorded.

events.title: Death of Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira
events.text: The founder dies at 86.

events.title: The succession dispute begins
events.text: The majority wing led by João Scognamiglio Clá Dias sues over the statute reserving voting rights to the nine founding members; about 80% of the 1,800 members side with it.

events.title: Heralds of the Gospel founded
events.text: Clá Dias founds the Arautos do Evangelho, canonically erected at diocesan level the same year.

events.title: Pontifical approval of the Heralds
events.text: John Paul II's Pontifical Council for the Laity recognizes the Heralds as an international private association of the faithful of pontifical right — the first such association approved by the Holy See in the third millennium (the precise formulation matters and is used here).

events.title: The courts award the TFP name
events.text: São Paulo courts give the entity, the TFP name and the patrimony to the wing linked to the Heralds; the founders' wing creates the Associação dos Fundadores (2004), later barred from using the TFP acronym; the STJ confirms non-founder voting rights, with a final appeal reaching the STF in 2013.

events.title: IPCO founded
events.text: Adolpho Lindenberg and disciples of the founders' wing create the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira — self-described heir of the original TFP line, at the historic headquarters.

events.title: The Heralds' clerical societies
events.text: The Heralds' societies Virgo Flos Carmeli (men) and Regina Virginum (women) are raised by Benedict XVI to societies of apostolic life; Clá Dias is ordained priest and made monsignor.

events.title: Apostolic visitation of the Heralds
events.text: The Vatican's congregation for consecrated life opens a visitation citing 'deficiencies in the style of government, formation, administration and fundraising', amid circulating videos of exorcism practices and statements about 'Dr. Plinio'; Clá Dias resigns the generalate on 12 June 2017.

events.title: Commissioner rejected by the Heralds' leadership
events.text: Francis names Cardinal Raymundo Damasceno Assis pontifical commissioner of the Heralds; the association's leadership under president Felipe Eugenio Lecaros Concha publicly declares the commissariat invalid — open conflict with the Vatican, alongside press accusations of physical, psychological and financial abuse (CartaCapital, NCR), which are attributed accusations.

events.title: The Heralds' schools ordered closed
events.text: The Vatican determines the closure of the Heralds' boarding schools, citing excessively rigid discipline and isolation from families — per NCR's reporting of the Vatican decision.

events.title: Ordinations resume; the documentary case
events.text: A single source reports the resumption of the Heralds' ordinations after a seven-year suspension — unverified, flagged; PT Wikipedia records the STF authorizing an HBO Max documentary on the group after an attempted judicial block.

events.title: The two branches today
events.text: The IPCO carries the founders' line (street campaigns, anti-'gender ideology', public rosaries); the Heralds continue under canonical supervision; the international network remains active — American TFP with TFP Student Action, TFP France with Avenir de la Culture, Germany's DVCK, Poland's Piotr Skarga association, the Fédération Pro Europa Christiana — each autonomous. Critical NGO reports on the network (EPF) are labeled as hostile sources.

figures.name: Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira
figures.role: Lay founder and lifelong leader: constituent deputy 1933–34, Catholic Action president 1940–44, Legionário director, PUC-SP history professor, founder of Catolicismo (1951) and the TFP (1960), author of 'Revolução e Contra-Revolução' (1959) and 'Nobreza e Elites Tradicionais Análogas' (1993). Historians examine anti-Jewish passages in his 1930s articles in A Ordem (attributed); he called Vatican II 'one of the greatest calamities in the history of the Church' (1976).

figures.name: Antônio de Castro Mayer
figures.role: Bishop of Campos (coadjutor 1948, diocesan 1949, resigned 1981); patron of Catolicismo; co-author of 'Reforma Agrária: Questão de Consciência'; broke with Plinio and the TFP in the 1980s (details a documented gap); co-consecrator at Écône 1988 → declared excommunication; died April 1991 — sources diverge between 25 and 26 April. The bridge figure to the fsspx project, where his Campos succession is charted.

figures.name: Geraldo de Proença Sigaud SVD
figures.role: Bishop of Jacarezinho 1947–60, archbishop of Diamantina 1960–80; secretary of the Coetus Internationalis Patrum; co-author of 'Reforma Agrária: QC'; broke with the TFP in 1970 and did not follow Lefebvre.

figures.name: João Scognamiglio Clá Dias
figures.role: Plinio's right hand in the TFP; leader of the majority wing after 1995; founder of the Heralds of the Gospel (1999); ordained priest (2005 per PT Wikipedia, ordination year flagged for verification) and made monsignor; resigned the generalate in June 2017 during the apostolic visitation; press accusations of abuse of authority and finances are attributed.

figures.name: Adolpho Lindenberg
figures.role: Renowned São Paulo engineer-architect, Plinio's cousin and disciple; TFP co-founder; founder and later honorary president of the IPCO; died 2 May 2024 at 99.

figures.name: Luiz Mendonça de Freitas
figures.role: Economist; fourth co-author of 'Reforma Agrária: Questão de Consciência' (the technical part).

figures.name: Luiz Sérgio Solimeo
figures.role: TFP member since 1959; writer of the American TFP's Sedes Sapientiae institute (movement sources).

figures.name: Felipe Eugenio Lecaros Concha
figures.role: Heralds' president elected 2019 (public role); protagonist of the refusal of the pontifical commissariat.

figures.name: Raymundo Damasceno Assis
figures.role: Cardinal; pontifical commissioner of the Heralds since 2019, with Bishop José Aparecido Gonçalves de Almeida and Sr. Marian Ambrosio.

figures.name: The episcopal critics
figures.role: The 1985 CNBB note commission — Gilberto Pereira Lopes (Campinas), Antonio Misiara (Bragança Paulista), Carlos Alberto Navarro (Campos); and historically Cardinal Carlos Carmelo de Vasconcelos Motta, who removed Plinio from his São Paulo posts in the 1940s.

organizations.name: TFP Brazil (1960)
organizations.relation: The original civil entity; judicial control passed in 2003–04 to the wing linked to the Heralds, which holds the name; low public activity of its own today (single-source, flagged).

organizations.name: The international TFP network
organizations.relation: Roughly 25–30 autonomous entities inspired by Plinio, coordinated via istfp.org: American TFP (with TFP Student Action and America Needs Fatima), TFP France/Avenir de la Culture, DVCK/TFP Deutschland, Poland's Stowarzyszenie Ks. Piotra Skargi, the Fédération Pro Europa Christiana (Brussels, 2008); extinct branches include Venezuela (~1986) and Spain/Argentina/Chile/Peru (~1998).

organizations.name: Heralds of the Gospel (1999/2001)
organizations.relation: International private association of the faithful of pontifical right, plus the societies of apostolic life Virgo Flos Carmeli and Regina Virginum (2009); under a pontifical commissioner since 2019.

organizations.name: Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira — IPCO (2006)
organizations.relation: Civil association of the founders' line; current campaigns against abortion, 'gender ideology' and communism.

organizations.name: Centro Dom Bosco (Rio, 2016)
organizations.relation: NOT a TFP entity: an independent lay traditionalist center; research notes sympathies and occasional cooperation with the IPCO — related, no organic link.

disambiguation.note: The TFP sits at crowded intersections of Brazilian traditionalism; these cards keep the lines straight.

items.title: TFP ≠ SSPX
items.text: The TFP is a LAY movement founded and led by a layman; the SSPX is a priestly fraternity (Lefebvre). The TFP did not adhere to the 1988 consecrations and remained formally in communion. Castro Mayer is the biographical bridge between the two worlds — co-author with Plinio in the 1950s–60s, co-consecrator at Écône in 1988; his line is charted in the fsspx project.

items.title: TFP vs Heralds vs IPCO
items.text: The Heralds spring from the TFP's post-1995 majority wing (Clá Dias) and hold canonical status; the IPCO represents the founders' minority wing, without canonical statute, heir of the original style. The courts gave the TFP name to the Clá Dias wing; symbolically both claim Plinio.

items.title: 'Counter-Revolution' is a technical term
items.text: In Plinio's 'Revolução e Contra-Revolução' (1959) the 'Revolution' is a five-century process (pseudo-Reformation → French Revolution → communism, later a 'fourth revolution' of culture) and the 'Counter-Revolution' its ordered reversal — definitions to be attributed to the text, not conflated with generic usage.

items.title: Two 'TFPs' today
items.text: The Brazilian civil entity of that name (Heralds' wing) and the international istfp/IPCO network are distinct — beware of citing 'the TFP' in the present tense without specifying which.

items.title: Accusations are attributed
items.text: The 'sect'/'slavery' accusations (Venezuela 1984, the French 1995 report, press investigations of the Heralds) produced no judicial conviction in the sources consulted; this site records them as attributed accusations together with the movement's replies.
